faqs.q: How much does a Russian Toy cost to buy?
faqs.a: Reputable breeders typically charge $500–$2,000 for a Russian Toy puppy. Prices vary by breeder reputation, health testing, and lineage. Rescue adoption fees are typically $100–$500 and include vaccinations, neutering, and microchipping.

faqs.q: What is the monthly cost of owning a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Budget $120–$200 per month for a Russian Toy, covering food, preventive vet care, insurance, grooming and supplies. Small breeds often cost less on food and some products, but vet bills don't proportionally reduce — procedures cost similar amounts regardless of size.

faqs.q: What are the biggest ongoing costs for a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: The three largest annual expenses are food ($300–600), veterinary care ($400–$1,200 budgeted annually), and pet insurance ($$400–$1,200 per year). Grooming costs are lower for short-coated breeds managed at home.

faqs.q: How much does a Russian Toy cost in the first year?
faqs.a: Year one costs for a Russian Toy are significantly higher than subsequent years, typically $1,500–$3,000. This covers the purchase price or adoption fee, initial vet checks, vaccinations, spay/neuter, microchipping, crate, bedding, collar, leads and puppy training classes.

faqs.q: How often should I groom a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Russian Toys need brushing once or twice per week.  Nails should be trimmed every 3–4 weeks. Ears should be checked and cleaned monthly.

faqs.q: Do Russian Toys shed a lot?
faqs.a: Russian Toys shed minimally. A weekly brush is usually sufficient.

faqs.q: What grooming tools does a Russian Toy need?
faqs.a: A rubber grooming glove or soft-bristle brush is sufficient for weekly maintenance on the Russian Toy's short coat. Add a nail grinder and ear cleaner for a complete grooming kit.

faqs.q: How often should I bathe a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Every 4–6 weeks is appropriate for most Russian Toys that live indoors. More frequent bathing is needed if they swim or spend time in mud. Over-bathing strips natural skin oils — use a pH-balanced dog shampoo rather than human products.

faqs.q: Are Russian Toys easy to train?
faqs.a: Russian Toys are considered easier to train than average — they respond quickly to reward-based methods and generalise cues well. Short 10–15 minute sessions outperform long correction-heavy drills.

faqs.q: What training method works best for a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Reward-based training using treats, praise and toy rewards is the most effective and well-researched approach for Russian Toys. Keep sessions short and positive, end on a success, and vary your rewards to maintain engagement.

faqs.q: At what age should I start training my Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Start training from the day your puppy arrives home, typically at 8 weeks. The 8–16 week window is the most sensitive socialisation period. Enrol in a puppy class within the first two weeks for structured socialisation alongside basic obedience foundations.

faqs.q: How long does it take to train a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Most Russian Toys learn basic obedience cues (sit, stay, come, down) within 2–4 weeks of daily practice. Reliable recall in distracting environments typically takes 2–3 months of consistent reinforcement.

faqs.q: What health problems do Russian Toys commonly have?
faqs.a: Russian Toys are most commonly associated with routine age-related conditions. Regular vet checks, appropriate weight management, and breed-specific screening tests help detect issues early. Ask any breeder for health test results before purchasing.

faqs.q: How long do Russian Toys live?
faqs.a: Russian Toys have an average lifespan of 12–14 years. Small breeds often live longer than large breeds. Dental care is particularly important for small dogs, as dental disease is a common longevity issue.

faqs.q: Are Russian Toys prone to hip dysplasia?
faqs.a: Hip dysplasia is less common in Russian Toys than in large working breeds, but it can still occur. Responsible breeders screen breeding stock. Keeping your Russian Toy at a healthy weight is the most effective preventive measure.

faqs.q: What health tests should a Russian Toy puppy have?
faqs.a: At minimum, your Russian Toy puppy should have a vet health check, first vaccinations, deworming, and microchipping before coming home. Ask the breeder for parent health certificates relevant to Russian Toy-specific conditions. A vet check within 72 hours of bringing your puppy home is recommended to establish a baseline.

faqs.q: Are Russian Toys good with kids?
faqs.a: Russian Toys can do well with children when properly socialised from puppyhood. Every dog is an individual — early exposure to children's behaviour (noise, sudden movements) is the most effective preparation.

faqs.q: Do Russian Toys get along with other dogs?
faqs.a: Russian Toys are generally sociable with other dogs, particularly when well-socialised from puppyhood. Introduce new dogs on neutral territory and keep initial meetings brief and positive.

faqs.q: Do Russian Toys bark a lot?
faqs.a: Russian Toys are not considered excessive barkers. They may alert to strangers or unusual sounds, but are generally manageable with basic training. Consistent "quiet" reinforcement from puppyhood keeps this in check.

faqs.q: Are Russian Toys good apartment dogs?
faqs.a: Russian Toys adapt reasonably well to apartment living, particularly if they receive consistent daily walks and indoor enrichment. Their compact nature makes them less disruptive in confined spaces than high-energy large breeds.

faqs.q: How much exercise does a Russian Toy need per day?
faqs.a: Russian Toys need approximately 45–60 minutes of exercise daily. A structured morning walk and an evening sniff walk usually cover their needs. Mental exercise (training sessions, puzzle feeders) counts toward overall stimulation needs and can reduce restless behaviour.

faqs.q: Are Russian Toys good running partners?
faqs.a: Russian Toys can join you for moderate runs once fully grown. They're better suited to steady 3–5 mile runs than extended distance. Watch for signs of fatigue and always run in cooler hours during summer.

faqs.q: What happens if a Russian Toy doesn't get enough exercise?
faqs.a: Russian Toys are less demanding than high-energy breeds, but chronic under-exercise still leads to weight gain and low-level restlessness. Even lower-energy breeds benefit from a consistent daily walk for both physical health and mental stimulation.

faqs.q: Can a Russian Toy be off-lead?
faqs.a: Russian Toys can be off-lead in secure areas once recall is reliable. Reliable recall typically takes 3–4 months of consistent training with progressive distance and distractions. Never trust off-lead recall in an unfenced area until it's been tested in controlled conditions first.

faqs.q: How much should I feed my Russian Toy?
faqs.a: A Russian Toy needs approximately ½–1½ cups of dry food per day for an adult, split across two meals. Always follow the feeding guide on your specific formula — calorie density varies significantly between brands. Adjust portions based on body condition: you should be able to feel (but not easily see) the ribs.

faqs.q: How many times a day should I feed a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Adult Russian Toys should eat twice daily. Puppies (under 6 months) need 3–4 smaller meals per day to support growth and prevent hypoglycaemia, particularly in small breeds.

faqs.q: What is the best food for a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Look for a formula carrying an AAFCO adequacy statement for the correct life stage. A named protein source (chicken, turkey, beef, salmon) should appear first in the ingredient list. Medium-energy Russian Toys do well on standard adult maintenance formulas with named protein as the first ingredient.

faqs.q: When should I switch my Russian Toy from puppy to adult food?
faqs.a: Small breeds typically transition to adult food around 12 months. Moving too late keeps them on higher-calorie puppy formulas that can cause weight gain in lower-activity adults.

faqs.q: Is a Russian Toy a good dog for first-time owners?
faqs.a: Russian Toys are generally considered suitable for first-time owners. They're responsive to training, manageable in size, and adaptable to different home environments. A puppy class is still recommended to build a strong foundation.

faqs.q: Are Russian Toys good family dogs?
faqs.a: Russian Toys can be good family dogs when properly socialised. Their suitability depends more on individual temperament and upbringing than breed alone.

faqs.q: Do Russian Toys do well when left alone?
faqs.a: Russian Toys form strong bonds with their owners and do not do well with extended isolation. Aim for no more than 4–6 hours alone at a time. If your schedule requires longer absences, consider a dog walker, doggy daycare, or a companion dog.

faqs.q: How much time do you need for a Russian Toy?
faqs.a: Plan for 1.5–2 hours per day dedicated to your Russian Toy — covering exercise, training, feeding and general interaction.  The commitment is consistent year-round, not just when convenient.
